source_document.body:
The Treaty Creek gold camp in northwest British Columbia. Credit: Tudor Gold Corp.
Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 24, 2026
Tudor Gold’s (TSXV: TUD; US-OTC: TDRRF) Goldstorm deposit in northwestern British Columbia could yield a $2.3 billion (C$3.2 billion) post-tax net present value at $1.54 billion in initial costs, the first economic assessment of its Treaty Creek project shows.
The Goldstorm mine, about 930 km northwest of Vancouver, could produce 4.68 million oz. of gold over 28 years with a 20% internal rate of return.
“We expect to receive our underground exploration permit in time to collar the portal and begin to excavate the decline in 2027,” Tudor President and CEO Joe Ovsenek said in a release. “With underground access to the Goldstorm deposit we can more efficiently infill drill and expand the higher-grade mineralization.”
The drilling would help pin down how much of the richer rock Tudor can count on, a significant task after the PEA. The junior miner must still secure permits and find financing for a project whose initial cost is more than nine times its market capitalization.
Resource base
Goldstorm’s 13.6 million inferred tonnes account for 14% of the 97.8 million tonnes in the mine plan but 29% of its gold. They grade 3.78 grams gold per tonne, more than twice the mine average of 1.8 grams gold. Tudor has yet to declare reserves.
Goldstorm’s November 2025 estimate outlined 912.3 million indicated tonnes grading 0.85 gram gold, 5.07 grams silver and 0.15% copper. That amounts to 24.9 million oz. of gold, 148.7 million oz. silver and 3.05 billion lb. copper.
Tudor shares fell 4.9% to C58¢ in Toronto on Tuesday afternoon, valuing the company at C$240 million. Tudor owns 80% of Treaty Creek and covers exploration costs for its 20% partner, Teuton Resources (TSXV: TUO; US-OTC: TEUTF), until it gives notice of production.
Higher grades first
Tudor would feed its 10,000-tonne-a-day mill from four zones, starting with some of the richest material. Gold output would average 202,300 oz. annually from years three through 12, at the low end of the 200,000 to 300,000 oz. range management was targeting in October. The life-of-mine average would be 165,600 oz. a year.
Vancouver-based Fuse Advisors assumed $3,670 per oz. gold, $50 per oz. silver and $5 per lb. copper. At those prices, the mine would pay back its initial costs in 3.7 years. Over its life, the mine would also yield 22.1 million oz. of silver and 209,900 tonnes of copper. After credits for both metals, all-in sustaining costs would average $1,358 per oz. of gold.
Tudor is looking to Perfectstorm, about 1 km west of Goldstorm, to lift early gold output. Hole PS-26-36 cut 9 grams gold over 9.5 metres from 163.5 metres downhole, Tudor reported Nov. 11. If next year’s drilling supports an initial resource by year-end, Tudor plans to study how to bring Perfectstorm into production.
Tunnel dispute
The proposed mill and some underground workings overlap with a provincial licence of occupation held by Seabridge Gold (TSX: SEA; NYSE: SA) for its neighbouring KSM project. Tudor may have to move or redesign those facilities unless the companies reach an agreement or the province changes the tenure, the study says.
B.C. has deferred a decision on permits for the full length of Seabridge’s proposed ore tunnels. About 12.5 km of the route crosses Tudor’s claims, passing through Goldstorm and Perfectstorm, Tudor says.
In a separate ruling , the B.C. Supreme Court confirmed last week that it had quashed the province’s finding that KSM construction had “substantially started.” B.C. must consult the Tsetsaut Skii km Lax Ha Nation in depth before making a new decision. KSM’s environmental certificate remains in force during the review, Seabridge said.

Porsche's ICE-Powered Macan Is Returning With a New Generation, Is This What It Will Look Like?
10 photos
Photo: Instagram | avarvarii
The original Porsche Macan lived for 12 years, with production spanning from 2014 to 2026, and that’s a very impressive achievement by today’s standards.
The company pulled the plug on it earlier this year, which is when the final copy rolled off the line at the Leipzig factory in Germany. It utilized the MLB platform, just like the old Audi Q5, the B8 A4, and its sportier-looking sibling, the A5, from the same era, and was offered with gasoline and diesel power throughout the years, with manual and automatic transmissions.
In case you forgot, there is an entirely new Porsche Macan out, and it is a battery-electric model. Production started two and a half years ago, in the first half of 2024, and it put together at the same facility as its ICE predecessor. The Macan EV utilizes the PPE (Premium Platform Electric) architecture, just like its larger sibling, the Cayenne Electric, as well as Audi’s A6 e-tron, and Q6 e-tron, and the Bentley Torcal.
Given that the Macan has officially transitioned to the battery-electric era, one might be tempted to think that there won’t be a combustion-powered alternative anymore. But they would be wrong, you see, because the Zuffenhausen company is indeed preparing such a thing as we speak. We have seen in on a few occasions, in the open, including last month (October 2026), and it is that prototype (it was actually a test mule) that has been used to create a set of realistic renderings.
Photo: Instagram | avarvarii The pixel artist behind the digital illustrations shared in the gallery above is none other than @avarvarii. As for the CGI-infused model, it looks pretty much like an evolution of its predecessor, which isn’t exactly a surprise given that this is after all Porsche, and it’s not famously known for significantly altering the looks of its new models compared to the older ones. And that’s definitely a compliment these days.
Don’t let the design trick you into thinking that it is another updated version of the first generation, because it isn’t. In fact, it will utilize the PPC (Premium Platform Combustion). The construction is the foundation stone of its lesser cousin, the new-gen Audi Q5, as well as the latest A5, A6, and Q7, and the first-ever Q9.
Power-wise, it should share some assemblies with the latest Audi Q5, and this probably means a straight-four and a V6 gasoline burner, and perhaps a TDI four-banger for the European market. In the States, you can get the Q5 with 268 hp from $53,300 (MSRP), and the SQ5 with 362 hp from $65,900. Chances are the new ICE-powered Macan will be punchier.
Reports indicate the new ICE -powered Porsche Macan will probably arrive in late 2028, and that’s two years from now. If that’s the case, then it should arrive in USA for the 2029 model year. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Avarvarii Automotive Artworks (@avarvarii)

Cadillac’s three-row electric SUV just got a little more expensive. The 2027 Cadillac Vistiq now starts at over $80,000.
2027 Cadillac Vistiq prices by trim
The Vistiq sits between the massive Escalade IQ and Lyriq as a “mini Escalade,” if you will, offering three rows of seating, but in a smaller, more affordable package.
Just a month ago, the 2027 Cadillac Vistiq was available starting at $79,495, but GM quietly raised prices.
As GM Authority uncovered on Cadillac’s website, prices for the base 2027 Vistiq Luxury are now listed from $80,395, or $900 more than last month. In fact, the Luxury, Premium Luxury, and Platinum models are all $900 more, while the Sport trim got a $1,000 price increase.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
While $900 won’t break the bank on a luxury three-row SUV, the cheapest 2027 Cadillac Vistiq Luxury trim now starts at over $80,000.
Like all 2027 GM electric vehicles, the Vistiq now has a built-in NACS charge port, so you don’t need a separate adapter to use at Tesla Superchargers.
2027 Cadillac Vistiq (Source: Cadillac)
The 2027 Cadillac Vistiq is available in four trims: Luxury, Sport, Premium Luxury, and Platinum. All are powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain that delivers a combined 615 hp and 650 lb-ft of torque.
Cadillac’s three-row electric SUV uses a 102 kWh battery, offering an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 305 miles on a single charge.
2027 Cadillac Vistiq interior (Source: Cadillac)
All trims come with a 33″ Horizon Display, Power driver and front passenger massage seats, a premium 23-speaker AKG Studio audio system, and a Power SkyGlass roof as standard.
At 205.6″ long, 79.7″ wide, and 71″ tall, with a 121.8″ wheelbase, the Vistiq is slightly longer but shorter than the Rivian R1S.

Vistiq Luxury | $80,395

This Tucker, Built After the Factory Closed, Sat Hidden for 13 Years, Great-Grandsons Bring It Home
17 photos
Photo: Preston Tucker's Speed Shop | YouTube
This 1948 Tucker was completed nearly 40 years after the Tucker factory permanently closed. Its body shell was stamped at the Chicago plant back in the late 1940s. The factory closed down in 1950, and the #1051 was not assembled into a finished, drivable car until the late 1980s.
The Tucker factory officially numbered its completed production cars sequentially from #1001 to #1050. Because Body #54 left the factory without an official chassis number, New Jersey car enthusiast and Air Force veteran Chick DeLorenzo, who had grown up in a Tucker dealership family, simply picked the very next number in sequence, #1051, when he finished building it in the late 1980s.
So the Tucker #1051 began as Body #54, one of eight unfinished car shells left behind when Preston Tucker's Chicago factory closed in 1949. Long story short, his build included a genuine, unused factory Tucker engine, which was originally a Franklin O-335 helicopter engine, and hand-crafted components.
After sitting hidden in a garage for 13 long years, it was bought in 2025 by Preston Tucker's great-grandsons, Mike and Sean, along with builder Rob Ida, finally bringing a factory-built Tucker body into the Tucker family.
Photo: Preston Tucker's Speed Shop | YouTube But it has been a bumpy road. After leaving the 1950 bankruptcy auction without a serial number, interior, or drivetrain, Body #54 passed through the hands of car collectors Ezra Schlipf of Metamora, Illinois, and Dewey Bloomquist of Sandwich, Illinois, before landing at the Poll Museum in Holland, Michigan.
For years, many assumed the bare shell was the missing factory car #1050, until factory body stampings proved it was actually Body #54. When Chick DeLorenzo acquired the unfinished car from the Poll Museum in 1986, it was a non-operational shell with loose hardware, delivered in bushel baskets. He simply refused to drop in a modern V8 and call it a day.
Instead, he tracked down a genuine leftover Franklin O-335 air-cooled helicopter engine converted to water-cooled by Tucker's engineers, engine #33584, the same powerplant Preston Tucker had adapted for the production cars, and paired it with a Cord pre-selector transmission.
Because exterior panels were extremely difficult to find, DeLorenzo molded his own fiberglass doors and fenders. For the wheel covers, he resorted to hand-spinning metal hubcaps on a lathe, pushing the metal against a form, leaving marks that are still visible today. He painted the car maroon over a tan interior after having been gray, red, and blue. It was August 1989 when he completed it.
Photo: Preston Tucker's Speed Shop | YouTube DeLorenzo passed away in January 2012, at the age of 76, and the car he completed spent years hidden in his garage in Butler, New Jersey. His family had tucked the Tucker #1051 away inside his Butler garage, where it remained unseen for 13 years. In the meantime, Preston Tucker's descendants had never owned a Tucker automobile .
In early 2025, his great-grandsons, Mike and Sean, teamed up with longtime family friend and custom car builder Rob Ida to purchase #1051 from the DeLorenzo family after keeping it tucked away for 13 years. The Tucker brothers got the call from the DeLorenzo family in December 2024. His daughter-in-law told them they were finally ready to let it go.
On pickup day , March 29, 2025, the team rolled the car into the sunlight for the first time since 2012. When Preston Tucker’s great-grandsons opened the front trunk of the Tucker #1051, they found a set of original vintage Tucker suitcases. Chick DeLorenzo had stored the set of custom Samsonite-style suitcases, complete with their original garment hangers, sold through the Tucker Accessories Program in 1948.
The trio trailered it to Ida's shop in Morganville, New Jersey. Without spark or fuel after such a long hibernation, the car was brought back to life, and the rear-mounted original Franklin engine roared again. They did everything that needed to be done to put the car back on the road.
Photo: Preston Tucker's Speed Shop | YouTube Since then, the Tucker has been exhibited at the Greenwich Concours d’Elegance on June 1, 2025, just two months after Preston Tucker's great-grandsons and Rob Ida pulled it out of its 13-year garage storage. The car was also spotted driving on the streets of New York City.
The Tucker #1051, tracked down by Preston Tucker’s great-grandsons, is not the last one built. There is also a Tucker #1052, formally cataloged as #1052C by the Tucker Automobile Preservation Society, which was completed in 2015.
Unlike #1051, which started as an unfinished factory body shell, #1052 was constructed around an original factory engineering test chassis, originally used to test Preston Tucker’s experimental automatic transmission in Chicago, using spare parts from several cars.
When Tucker's assets were liquidated in 1950, collector Ezra Schlipf also acquired this test chassis. In the following years, it passed through the hands of collectors. It was completed in 2015 and named "Sofie," after Preston Tucker’s mother.

Great on any Friday: Ecoflow River 3 Plus - Portable Power Station, 286Wh LiFePO4 Battery
Insider Confirms That the 8.0-Liter Power Stroke Diesel Is Coming and Ford Has a Name for It
7 photos
Photo: Ford
The rumor mill has been spinning for months. Now, here comes the confirmation. An insider says the speculation has a real basis. While Ford hasn't made an official announcement, the 8.0-liter Power Stroke turbo-diesel is reportedly coming, and Ford has come up with an internal code name for it.
For the 2027 model year, Ford reduced its heavy-duty Super Duty engine lineup for the F-250, F-350, and F-450 down to just two V8 powerplants: the 7.3-liter Godzilla gas V8 and the 6.7-liter High-Output Power Stroke turbo-diesel V8. Ford dropped its previous entry-level 6.8-liter gas V8 and the Standard-Output 6.7-liter diesel.
The 6.7-liter Scorpion High-Output Power Stroke produces 500 horsepower (507 metric horsepower) and a massive 1,200 pound-feet (1,627 Newton meters) of torque, while the 7.3-liter Godzilla makes do with 420 horsepower (426 metric horsepower) and 445 pound-feet (603 Newton meters).
Now, it seems that Ford has another engine in the making. The automaker has reportedly sent it into the testing phase, an insider confirmed for The Fast Lane Truck YouTube channel. The insider also revealed the name of the engine. Ford is referring to it as the "Roadrunner."
Photo: Ford Unofficial reports claim that it will come with between 550 and 650 horsepower (between 558 and 659 metric horsepower) and roughly 1,400 - 1,500 pound-feet (1,898 - 2,034 Newton meters) of torque, which will position it at the top of the lineup. A twin-turbo setup designed to build boost quickly at low rpm, while sustaining airflow under heavy towing loads, should be part of the plan.
This comes after earlier this year, TFL Truck dismissed the 8.0-liter V8 rumors as unverified internet speculation because there were no patents, no official Ford comments, and no mention of the engine in the 2027 Super Duty order guide. What the reliable source told them is now reversing their skepticism.
The Roadrunner will be an 8.0-liter Power Stroke turbo-diesel, with an engine capacity that will place it at the top of the range. But since the 2027 Super Duty lineup is already locked in, an 8.0-liter Roadrunner would most likely debut with the 2028 or even 2029 model year, alongside a major truck lineup redesign.
The Roadrunner is reportedly in active bench and prototype testing. Ford could offer the 8.0-liter as a heavy-towing upgrade above the 6.7-liter High-Output, similar to how it previously sold both the Standard-Output and the High-Output diesels, or possibly use it to replace the 6.7-liter entirely to meet stricter emissions standards. Up until then, the 6.7-liter High-Output Power Stroke remains Ford's sole heavy-duty diesel option.
Photo: Ford However, until Ford files public patents, releases the official specs, or lists the engine in a future order guide, the 8.0-liter remains a rumor rather than a guaranteed production engine. The move does make sense.
Ford would thus respond to competitors that scaled up their engine displacement. General Motors is reportedly developing an 8.3-liter Duramax (Mongoose), while Ram is rumored to have a 7.2-liter Cummins in the works.

Teen Gearhead Scores 1966 Ford Thunderbird Parked for 20 Years, Big Underhood Surprise Is Too Much
34 photos
Photo: YouTube/TDM Garage
Typically, classic cars find a loyal following within a demographic that’s closer in age to the respective cars, but notable, positive exceptions exist. Case in point: a sixty-year-old personal luxury car rescued by a GenZ-er is not the regular cars and coffee topic. But pulling a 60s Ford Thunderbird out of retirement is guaranteed to get a conversation started, regardless of the fact that the rescuer is still writing his teen age with a “1.”
Nothing screams classic car optimism quite like buying a dormant 1966 Ford Thunderbird sight unseen off Facebook Marketplace and expecting it to cooperate before lunch. That is exactly what the young gearhead behind the TDM Garage YouTube channel did after snatching this California cruiser out of San Leandro for $3,200, knocked down from $3,900. Last tagged in April 2006, it had slumbered for 20 years—longer than its wrencher errant has been alive.
The listing proudly promised the two-door had been sitting indoors, making the sun-baked surface rust blanketing its roof, decklid, and door tops a masterclass in creative copywriting. Below that beltline, however, the Medium Sage Gold Metallic Town Hardtop remains remarkably straight on black steel wheels and whitewall tires, complete with black-and-yellow RNS 535 plates, a College of San Mateo bumper sticker, a missing gas cap, and one front hub bravely rocking four lug studs.
Swinging open the massive door reveals a jet-age cockpit packed with four recessed gauge pods, a Swing-Away steering wheel, factory air conditioning, steering-wheel speed control, and a reclining passenger seat buried beneath 1958-to-1966 Thunderbird Headquarters catalogs. Someone previously yanked the back seat out just to break into the jammed trunk, the headliner tickles your scalp. The brake pedal refuses to budge, yet the driver's side power windows still zip smoothly.
Photo: YouTube/TDM Garage Even the mileage brings comedic flair, with the seller typing 99,999 miles while the odometer shows roughly 46,000 miles. Never mind the cosmetic scars or frozen brakes—stopping is strictly a problem for future Tuesday—because popping the hood exposes the real jackpot . Wedged beneath California Thermactor smog plumbing and a hefty air-conditioning compressor sits a factory Q-code 428-cubic-inch V8 bolted to a 3-speed Cruise-O-Matic automatic transmission, and a 3.00:1 rear axle.
Revival day began with automotive musical chairs, juggling two batteries across five yard cars before scrubbing corroded cables and the radiator-mounted solenoid. Turning the key yielded dead silence until the host realized the misadjusted column shifter refused Park, likely stumping the last mechanic. Wiggling into Neutral outsmarted the safety switch and woke the starter, letting him oil accessible cylinders, clean the points, and hunt down a buried dipstick revealing clean, full oil.
A bone-dry surge tank and a water-bottle test confirmed a dead mechanical fuel pump buried behind the fan, pulleys, and power steering. Whispering that this 428 might eventually migrate into a Shelby anyway, he skipped tearing the front apart and fed the four-barrel carburetor starting fluid.
Photo: YouTube/TDM Garage The 7.0-liter V8 cranked and sounded like it would gladly kick its pistons into reciprocating, but something is definitely off. There may be no spark, or the distributor gets its timing dead wrong, or fuel doesn’t reach the combustion chamber – the young gearhead has his work cut out for him, that’s a strong fact we can infer from the video.
Day 2 brought an auxiliary fuel bottle, hose clamps, and a brass shut-off valve, transforming the brave savior into a self-proclaimed plumber rigging a gravity-feed IV drip straight into the carburetor. Gas reached the inlet, yet clogged internals stubbornly refused to drink it. With a week-long rainstorm rolling in just an hour away, he dismantled the rig before creating a live bomb, still beaming over a thrilling triumph: the big V8 lives after 20 silent years.
Waking a neglected Thunderbird hits harder once you recall its towering Detroit legacy. Launched for 1955 as Ford's two-seat V8 reply to Chevrolet's Corvette, the Thunderbird effectively invented the personal luxury car by trading track harshness for boulevard glamour. Across eleven generations from 1955 to 1997 and a retro encore from 2002 to 2005, Ford built over 4.4 million units, peaking at 352,751 in 1978 during fuel-crisis panic and bottoming out at 9,295 in 2005.
Photo: YouTube/TDM Garage By 1966, the fourth-generation Flair Bird took its final bow with 69,176 cars built across four body styles. The vinyl-topped Town Landau dominated at 35,105 units, followed by 15,633 blind-pillar Town Hardtops like this survivor, 13,389 Hardtop Coupes, and 5,049 Convertibles.
With no manual gearbox offered, the standard Z-code 390-cube V8 produced 315 hp at 4,600 rpm and 427 lb-ft at 2,800 rpm, pushing the 4,400-pound cruiser to 60 mph in roughly 10 seconds and 17-second quarters. Ordering the 428 cut 0-to-60 mph to around 8.5 seconds, ran 16-second quarters, and hit 120 mph. While the cheapest Hardtop started at $4,426, this Town Hardtop listed at $4,483 plus $86 for the 428—$4,569 before options.
That optional big-block deserves its own standing ovation. Debuting for 1966 and retiring after 1970, Ford's 428-cubic-inch cast-iron FE V8 paired a 4.13-inch bore with a 3.98-inch stroke and 10.5:1 compression, delivering effortless street torque where the high-strung racing 427 proved temperamental.
Photo: YouTube/TDM Garage It arrived first in the 1966 Thunderbird, full-size Fords led by the Galaxie 500 7-Litre and LTD, Mercury's full-size fleet headlined by the one-year-only S-55 Super Marauder, and law-enforcement Police Interceptors.
Across every civilian 1966 application—Thunderbird, Galaxie 7-Litre, full-size Ford, and Mercury S-55—the single-four-barrel Q-code 428 shared identical ratings of 345 hp at 4,600 rpm and 462 lb-ft of torque at 2,800 rpm. Car Life timed an automatic Galaxie 7-Litre from 0 to 60 mph in 8.0 seconds with a 16.4-second quarter-mile at 89 mph, while 4-speed Mercury S-55 models dipped into the low 7-second range and mid-15s despite hauling full-size bulk.
Ford also slipped law enforcement the 1966 P-code 428 Police Interceptor, packing solid lifters, a hotter cam, and an aluminum intake for 360 hp at 5,400 rpm, 459 lb-ft at 3,200 rpm, and speeds past 128 mph.
Later came Carroll Shelby 's 355-hp GT500 units and the 1968.5-to-1970 Cobra Jet and Super Cobra Jet derivatives of the 428, hilariously underrated at 335 hp and 440 lb-ft in Mustangs, Torinos, Fairlanes, Cougars, and Cyclones.

1965 Ferrari 275 GTS Spent Over 40 Years in Hiding, Sells for Nearly $1 Million
10 photos
Photo: Christie's
Ferraris are some of the most desirable classic cars out there, with many of them worth millions of dollars . They usually get pampered a lot. However, while many of them reside in museums and fancy collections, others have been hidden from sight for decades. This 1965 275 GTS is one such vehicle.
This Ferrari was recently auctioned off via Christie's at Retromobile New York Auctions. It crossed the block in late November 2026. The event marked its first public appearance in over four decades. And despite not being driven for so long, the 275 GTS is still in pretty good condition, especially for an unrestored survivor.
Although it didn't have a rough life, this Italian drop-top didn't get a lot of maintenance either. The iconic red paint is faded, weathered, and even cracked in places, with some surface rust visible on the trunk lid, the nose, and the lower sides.
The soft top is quite dirty as well, while the door panels look like they haven't been cared for since the car rolled off the showroom floor. The interior could use new carpets, while the tan seats need a much-deserved cleaning. Everything else appears to be fine, though; I haven't spotted cracks on the dash and steering, and there are no missing bits and pieces to run by.
As for the V12 engine, it's as original as they get, and it has plenty of dust and grime to brag about. Much like the interior, this engine bay hasn't been detailed. The car crossed the block with a few extra parts, including a front end, bumpers, headlamps, and chrome trim.
It's unclear if the car was originally shipped to the US, but existing documents show that it's been on this side of the Atlantic since 1979. That's when it was purchased by Ferrari enthusiast Charlie Kemp. He sold it later that year to a gentleman named Richard Watkins, who kept it in Richmond, Virginia until 1980.
Then it found its way to another Ferrari enthusiast, Barbour Byrd Wilson, who kept it in Hudson, Wisconsin, from 1980 to 2006. The previous owner kept it for two decades, until the Ferrari changed hands at the recent New York auction.
Speaking of which, the Ferrari was estimated to fetch between $1 million and $1.2 million, but it eventually sold for $995,000. The sum likely includes a buyer's premium.
Introduced in 1964 as a replacement for the 250 GTO, the Ferrari 275 series spawned models like the GTB, GTS, GTB/4, and the GTS/4 NART. Several cars were modified for racing.
The GTS was a convertible version of the GTB , but it had quite a few unique features, including a shorter front hood and smaller uncovered headlamps. Mechanically, it was virtually identical to the GTB, but the 3.3-liter V12 engine was slightly less potent at 260 horsepower. Ferrari produced only 200 units between late 1964 and early 1966.
Examples in excellent condition typically go for seven-figure sums. As of this writing, the five most expensive 275 GTS models fetched between $1.87 and $2.36 million. Three units fetched over $2 million since 2025.

Oil prices are in the middle of a massive reset and the benchmark price that is the basis for most fuel surcharges is rapidly reflecting those changes.
The Department of Energy/Energy Information Administration average retail diesel price declined 24.2 cents/gallon to $5.695/g, effective Monday but published Tuesday. That is the largest one-week decline since the Iran war began.
It’s also the fourth consecutive week of a falling benchmark price. The total decline during that time is 65.7 cts/g.
It put the price 83.4 cts/g less than it was September 22, when it hit its all-time high at $6.529/g. It’s also the lowest level since August 31.
However, this week’s price is still $1.798/g more than where it stood on March 2, the final DOE/EIA price published before the impact of the start of the Iran war over the prior weekend.
Retail prices always lag changes in futures and wholesale prices, so even the big drop posted this week doesn’t fully reflect just how much prices have come down in the futures market.
With November coming to a close, the scope of the fall in ultra low sulfur diesel (ULSD) on the CME commodity exchange this month becomes more striking.
ULSD settled November 2, the first trading day of the month, at $4.4216/g. A day later, it reached its high settlement for November at $4.5306/g. That followed an October where the average settlement was $4.79/g.
But as no new major military flareups occurred during the month, and a U.S. election that signaled U.S. exhaustion with the Iran war, prices began to fall.
On Wednesday, October 18, ULSD settled at less than $4/g for the first time since August. Three days later on Monday, ULSD hit its low settlement for November at $3.6975/g.
An increase of 0.55 cts/g Tuesday was the first time the price had risen in eight trading sessions.
Softening spread
What should also give diesel consumers additional relief is that the spread between diesel and crude, which hit stunning levels earlier in the recent cycle, is starting to soften.
The spread between world crude benchmark Brent and second-month ULSD on the CME settled Monday at about 63.7 cts/g. It opened the month at 77.3 cts/g and was consistently between 90 cts/g and $1/g through August.
But the push by refiners around the globe to cash in on strong refining margins, combined with signs pointing to a price-driven softening of demand, is weakening that spread. That’s good news for diesel consumers who at the peak of the spread blowing out wondered why the numbers they were hearing about increases in the price of crude were growing at a slower rate than what they were paying at the pump for their fuel.
Refiners working hard
U.S. refiners are working at maximum operating rates. The 95.7% operating rate for U.S. refiners in the week ending November, the latest data available, appears to be the highest in history for the second week of November.
The change in diesel inventories not just in the U.S. but worldwide is reflected in the difference between the first month and second ULSD price on CME.
That spread is in a structure known as backwardation, where the first month contract traded–December–is higher than the second month contract. It reflects the fact that the barrel for most immediate delivery is the one most desired in a tight market. It also discourages inventory-building.
The reverse of that is called contango. That is the structure where prices rise as they go out the calendar. It is the structure found in a perfectly-balanced market to reflect the costs of storage and the time value of money, and it reflects adequate inventories. If the stocks get too high, that contango will widen.
In the ULSD contract on CME, the spread between the first and second month contract settled Monday at 5.29 cts/g. That was the amount that December ULSD exceeded January ULSD.
That was the lowest level since July. It has averaged just over 9 cts/g for the month so far.
